prompt: DIN MIDI runs at 31,250 baud, so one bit lasts 32 µs. Why does the MIDI specification give 320 µs per byte rather than 256 µs for eight bits?

options.text: Each byte is framed by a start bit and a stop bit, so ten bit times pass on the wire
options.explanation: Correct. 8-N-1 framing adds a start bit and a stop bit to the eight data bits, and CA-033 states 10 bits and 320 µs per serial byte.

options.text: MIDI adds a parity bit and a stop bit
options.explanation: MIDI uses no parity. The two extra bit times are the start and stop bits.

options.text: The receiver's opto-isolator adds 64 µs to every byte
options.explanation: The 320 µs figure is wire time from framing. The specification asks for opto-isolator rise and fall times under 2 µs.

options.text: MIDI sends each byte MSB first and then repeats the top bits
options.explanation: UART data bits are sent LSB first, once each. There is no repetition.

workedExample:
1. A UART frame starts with a start bit (0), then eight data bits sent LSB first, then a stop bit (1).
2. That is ten bit times per byte; at 32 µs each, a byte occupies 320 µs, as CA-033 states.
3. The start and stop bits carry no payload but still take wire time, so DIN MIDI carries at most 3,125 bytes per second.

link.title: MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update (CA-033) — MIDI Association

prompt: A keyboard plays a four-note chord as four separate three-byte note-on messages over DIN MIDI, without running status. Your synth starts each voice as soon as its message is parsed. What should you expect?

options.text: The voices start one after another, with the last note-on finishing roughly 3.8 ms after the first byte began; running status would shorten this
options.explanation: Correct. Twelve bytes at 320 µs each arrive in sequence. Running status omits repeated status bytes, cutting the chord to nine bytes.

options.text: All four voices start together, because MIDI sends chord notes simultaneously
options.explanation: DIN MIDI is a single serial line: bytes, and therefore notes, arrive one after another.

options.text: A faster synth CPU removes the stagger
options.explanation: The stagger comes from wire time. Faster processing cannot start a note before its bytes have arrived.

options.text: The stagger is about 12 ms, one millisecond per byte
options.explanation: A MIDI byte takes 320 µs, not 1 ms; about 1 ms is a whole three-byte message.

workedExample:
1. DIN MIDI is one serial line, so the 12 bytes arrive one after another.
2. Each byte takes 320 µs, so each note-on completes about 0.96 ms after the previous one and the chord arrives in about 3.8 ms.
3. Running status cuts the chord to 9 bytes, about 2.9 ms.
4. The smear is small but real, and it belongs in the end-to-end latency budget.

link.title: MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update (CA-033) — MIDI Association

prompt: Why can't you connect a 5-pin DIN MIDI IN jack straight to a microcontroller's UART RX pin?

options.text: MIDI uses 9 data bits, which MCU UARTs cannot receive
options.explanation: MIDI uses eight data bits with 8-N-1 framing. Select a UART that supports that documented configuration; nine-bit framing is not the reason for the isolation circuit.

options.text: MIDI is a 5 mA current loop and the spec requires an opto-isolator at MIDI IN, so this MIDI data connection does not require a galvanic signal-ground connection
options.explanation: Correct. The receiver must use an opto-isolator, and the MIDI IN jack's pin 2 must have no DC path to the receiver's ground. A direct wire breaks that isolation.

options.text: The MIDI baud rate is too fast for an MCU UART
options.explanation: Select a UART that supports 31,250 baud within tolerance. Baud rate is not the reason DIN MIDI needs its specified isolation/interface circuit.
MIDI carries digital event data, not audio.

workedExample:
From CA-033:

1. 'The MIDI circuit is a 5mA current loop.'
2. Transmitter and receiver are 'separated by an opto-isolator' to avoid ground loops.
3. MIDI IN pin 2 'shall not have any DC path to the receiver's ground'.

So the RX pin connects to the opto-isolator's output, not to the jack.

link.title: MIDI 1.0 Electrical Specification Update (CA-033) — MIDI Association

prompt: A home-made MIDI receiver decodes the first bits of each byte correctly but gets the last bits wrong and reports framing errors. Its UART was set to 28,800 baud (a standard PC rate) instead of 31,250. Why do the errors concentrate at the end of each byte?

options.text: MIDI requires parity, which was disabled
options.explanation: MIDI is 8-N-1: no parity. Parity is not the issue.

options.text: 28,800 baud is too slow for the opto-isolator
options.explanation: The opto-isolator sees the sender's 31.25 kbaud edges regardless of the receiver's setting; the problem is where the receiver samples.

options.text: The bytes arrive in the wrong order
options.explanation: A UART cannot reorder bytes; it misreads bits within a byte.

options.text: With no clock wire, the receiver times every bit from the start edge; its bit period is about 8.5% too long, so the error accumulates and by the last bits it samples in the wrong bit
options.explanation: Correct. Each bit's sample point drifts a little further. Near the start the drift is tiny; by the stop bit it approaches a whole bit, so late bits and the stop bit are misread (framing error).

workedExample:
1. With no clock wire, the receiver times every bit from the start bit's falling edge, aiming for the middle of each bit.
2. At 28,800 baud the receiver's bit period is about 34.7 µs instead of 32 µs: about 8.5% too long.
3. The error adds up with every bit. By data bit D5 the sampling point has drifted more than half a bit, so it reads a neighbouring bit. By the stop bit the drift is most of a bit, so it can sample the wrong level and report a framing error.
4. The specification sets the MIDI rate at 31,250 baud ±1%, so configure exactly 31,250 baud.
